chief_complaint: honey-colored crusted erosions around mouth and nostrils in a 7-year-old boy (Impetigo Contagiosa)
hpi_details: 7-year-old boy brought by mother with a 5-day history of a spreading rash around his mouth and nose. Started as small red pimples and blisters that quickly burst, leaving behind moist, raw red patches covered with a thick, golden, 'honey-colored' crust. Lesions are mildly itchy and child constantly scratches them, causing new patches to appear on his chin and fingers. No fever or systemic illness.
ideas: mother thinks it is a cold sore or bad food allergy rash from eating strawberries
concerns: mother worried because the rash is spreading across his face and fingers rapidly
expectations: wants antibiotic ointment and note for school clearing him to return

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Non-Bullous Impetigo is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes topical antibiotic therapy with crust removal and hygiene counseling, escalating to oral antibiotics for widespread or bullous disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: honey-colored crusted erosions around mouth and nostrils in a 7-year-old boy (Impetigo Contagiosa)

Key HPI features: 7-year-old boy brought by mother with a 5-day history of a spreading rash around his mouth and nose. Started as small red pimples and blisters that quickly burst, leaving behind moist, raw red patches covered with a thick, golden, 'honey-colored' crust. Lesions are mildly itchy and child constantly scratches them, causing new patches to appear on his chin and fingers. No fever or systemic illness.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 84, Temp 36.8C. Perioral, perinasal, and dorsal hand skin examination reveals multiple confluent, shallow, erythematous erosions covered by distinctive adherent, golden-yellow ('honey-colored') crusts. No intact large bullae (excluding bullous impetigo). Regional submandibular lymphadenopathy present and mildly tender. Systemic exam completely normal.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Non-Bullous Impetigo.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Herpes simplex virus infection (cold sore) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or spreading redness — suggests progression to cellulitis, needing oral antibiotics.
management_principles: Localized therapy: for localized non-bullous impetigo with limited lesions, prescribe topical Mupirocin 2% ointment (or Retapamulin 1% ointment) applied to all affected areas TID for 5-7 days
Hygiene instructions: gently wash crusted areas with warm soapy water to remove crusts before ointment application; enforce strict handwashing and short fingernails to prevent autoinoculation
School exclusion counseling: child is highly contagious and must remain home from school/daycare until 24 hours after initiating topical antibiotic therapy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: honey-colored crusted erosions around mouth and nostrils in a 7-year-old boy (Impetigo Contagiosa)

7-year-old boy brought by mother with a 5-day history of a spreading rash around his mouth and nose. Started as small red pimples and blisters that quickly burst, leaving behind moist, raw red patches covered with a thick, golden, 'honey-colored' crust. Lesions are mildly itchy and child constantly scratches them, causing new patches to appear on his chin and fingers. No fever or systemic illness.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 84, Temp 36.8C. Perioral, perinasal, and dorsal hand skin examination reveals multiple confluent, shallow, erythematous erosions covered by distinctive adherent, golden-yellow ('honey-colored') crusts. No intact large bullae (excluding bullous impetigo). Regional submandibular lymphadenopathy present and mildly tender. Systemic exam completely normal.
reference_soap.assessment: Non-Bullous Impetigo Contagiosa secondary to Staphylococcus aureus and/or Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Localized therapy: for localized non-bullous impetigo with limited lesions, prescribe topical Mupirocin 2% ointment (or Retapamulin 1% ointment) applied to all affected areas TID for 5-7 days. 2. Hygiene instructions: gently wash crusted areas with warm soapy water to remove crusts before ointment application; enforce strict handwashing and short fingernails to prevent autoinoculation. 3. School exclusion counseling: child is highly contagious and must remain home from school/daycare until 24 hours after initiating topical antibiotic therapy. (If lesions become widespread or bullous, prescribe oral Cephalexin or Dicloxacillin).

learning_objectives: Recognize the pathognomonic clinical appearance of Non-Bullous Impetigo (adherent golden 'honey-colored' crusting over shallow facial/extremity erosions)

Differentiate Non-Bullous Impetigo (S. aureus or Group A Strep) from Bullous Impetigo (exclusively S. aureus producing exfoliative toxin A causing fragile clear flaccid bullae with collarette of scale)

Select appropriate topical antibiotic regimens (Mupirocin or Retapamulin ointment) for localized disease vs oral beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins/cephalosporins (Cephalexin) for widespread infection
Provide clear infection control and school return guidelines (excludable until 24 hours after starting effective antimicrobial therapy)

teaching.one_liner: A superficial bacterial skin infection, common in children, causing small blisters that quickly burst and dry into a characteristic golden 'honey-colored' crust around the mouth and nose.
red_flags: Fever or spreading redness — suggests progression to cellulitis, needing oral antibiotics

must_ask.say: Does the rash have a golden, honey-colored crust?
How did this start, and has it spread to other areas?
Is it itchy, and has he been scratching it?
Has he been in close contact with anyone with a similar rash?

history.answer: My son developed a raw rash with yellow crusts around his mouth and nose over the past five days.
It started five days ago as small red bumps around his mouth that turned into tiny blisters and popped, turning into these thick yellow crusts.
It began right around his lips and nose, but now it has spread down to his chin and onto the backs of his fingers.
They look like red raw patches covered in thick, sticky golden honey-colored crusts.
He says the sores itch a bit, but they do not really hurt unless he picks at them, and there was no pain before the rash appeared.
He scratches them constantly throughout the day, and everywhere his fingers touch, new sores seem to pop up a day or two later.
No, the sores stay in the same place and form crusts; they do not come and go within a few hours like hives.
No, his skin has always been smooth and clear, and he has never had sores like this before.
No, he has had no fever, chills, fatigue, or body aches at all; he has been acting and playing normally.
No, his lips, gums, tongue, and the inside of his mouth look totally clean, and his eyes are not red or sore.
No, the skin is not peeling off in sheets, and there are no dark purple spots that fail to fade when pressed.
No, his lips and tongue are not swollen, and he has had no trouble breathing, wheezing, or throat tightness.
He has not taken any new prescription medications, antibiotics, or pain relievers recently.
He ate fresh strawberries last weekend, so I wondered if this was a bad strawberry allergy or maybe a cold sore, but he had no other symptoms.
I noticed one of his classmates had a scabby sore on his face last week, and they sit together during art class.
No, we have not been hiking, he has not had any bug bites, and we have not traveled or visited a public swimming pool.
He has never had eczema, asthma, or hay fever, and he does not have sensitive skin.
No, his joints are completely fine with no swelling, and his fingernails look entirely normal.
I tried putting a little petroleum jelly and hydrocortisone cream on it two days ago, but it did not help and the crusts kept spreading.
I was wondering if this could be a cold sore from a virus, or maybe an allergic reaction to strawberries.
I am really worried because it is spreading so quickly across his face and onto his fingers.
I was hoping you could give us an antibiotic ointment to clear it up and a doctor's note so he can safely go back to school.
He has been completely healthy with no chronic medical conditions.
He has never had surgery and has never been admitted to a hospital.
He does not take any regular prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or daily supplements.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
No one smokes inside our house or around him.
He is a seven-year-old child, so alcohol does not apply.
He is in the second grade in elementary school and lives at home with me, his father, and his younger sister.
Neither my husband, my daughter, nor I have any skin sores or rashes right now, and there is no family history of skin disease.
He was born full-term by normal spontaneous vaginal delivery without any complications.
He has grown well along his normal percentiles and his childhood vaccinations are completely up to date.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, pulse 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable, well-nourished boy interacting normally with his mother, without acute distress.
Sclerae anicteric and conjunctivae clear, without injection, exudate, or discharge.
Oral mucosa, tongue, and posterior pharynx are pink and moist without erosions, vesicles, ulcers, or erythema; nasal mucosa is pink without mucosal lesions.
Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes are mildly enlarged, mobile, and mildly tender to palpation, with no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Multiple confluent, shallow erythematous erosions covered with thick, adherent golden-yellow honey-colored crusts around the mouth, nostrils, chin, and dorsal fingers; no large bullae, target lesions, or generalized rash.
Normal chest expansion with clear and equal breath sounds bilaterally, with no wheezes or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender, with no hepatosplenomegaly or masses.
Age-appropriate physical growth and developmental milestones with normal height and weight percentiles.
